questions.question: What is destructuring assignment and what are its main patterns?
questions.title: Destructuring Basics
questions.direct_answer: Destructuring unpacks values from arrays or properties from objects into distinct variables in one statement. Object: `const {a, b: renamed, c = default} = obj` — pulls by KEY, order-free. Array: `const [x, , z, ...rest] = arr` — pulls by POSITION, supports skipping. Extras: nested destructuring, rest elements collecting the remainder, function-parameter destructuring with defaults (the options-object idiom).

sections.title: Interview Answer
Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    O[obj] -->|by KEY| OD{a, b:renamed, c=5, ...rest}
    A[arr] -->|by POSITION| AD{x, hole, z, ...rest}
    OD --> P[function params: options idiom]
    AD --> S[swap, iterate protocol]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The two syntaxes are distinct protocols (the internals): object destructuring reads via property access (Get) — `{a} = obj` is `obj.a`; array destructuring reads via the ITERATOR protocol — `[x, y] = iterable` consumes iterator.next() twice. Consequence: array destructuring works on ANY iterable (strings, Maps, generators, Sets), and destructuring with holes (`, ,`) still CONSUMES values — `const [a, , c] = gen()` advances the generator twice for the skipped slot.

The computed-key and alias forms (the rarely-known depth): `const { [key]: value } = obj` destructures with a dynamic key; `const { a: { b: deep } } = obj` chains renaming into nesting. Combined with defaults at every level, this powers safe config drilling: `const { db: { host = 'localhost', port = 5432 } = {} } = config` — survives missing db entirely.

The design comparison (the judgment layer): destructuring vs property access is readability vs explicitness — repeated `obj.field` chains make the source obvious but noisy; destructuring states the contract up front (what this code NEEDS from the input) which is why it pairs with TypeScript types as a function's self-documentation. The lint rule that follows: prefer destructuring in parameter lists for functions with 3+ options, keep dot-access for 1–2 ad-hoc reads.
